**Given:** The finite binary state spaces, parameters and energy in the Definition, with AC for the library's conditional-independence convention.

[F1] A random element is a measurable map on a probability space, so the visible and hidden coordinate maps are random elements of finite spaces. [[def-random-element-and-real-random-variable]].

[F2] Conditional independence given a sigma-algebra means factorization of conditional expectations for every pair of bounded measurable real functions. [[def-conditional-independence-given-a-sigma-algebra]].

[F3] Expectation of an integrable random variable is its Lebesgue integral; on a finite probability space it is the finite weighted sum used in the Definition. [[def-expectation-of-a-nonnegative-or-integrable-random-variable]].

[A1] AC is the explicit hypothesis of the conditional-independence convention, and here means that every family of nonempty sets has a choice function. [[def-conditional-independence-given-a-sigma-algebra]] [[def-axiom-of-choice]].



**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 The state space $\{0,1\}^m\times\{0,1\}^n$ has $2^{m+n}$ elements. Every term $\exp(-E(v,h))$ is finite and positive, so their finite sum $Z$ is finite and positive; therefore $p$ is a probability mass function. [given, construct, algebra]

2.1 For fixed $v$, put $c_j=b_j+(W^Tv)_j$. Then $\exp(-E(v,h))=\exp(a^Tv)\prod_j\exp(h_jc_j)$, and summing over binary $h$ gives $\exp(a^Tv)\prod_j(1+\exp(c_j))$. Thus $p(h\mid v)$ is the product of Bernoulli masses with success probabilities $\exp(c_j)/(1+\exp(c_j))=\sigma(c_j)$. [given, step 1.1, algebra]

2.2 For fixed $h$, put $d_i=a_i+(Wh)_i$. Then $\exp(-E(v,h))=\exp(b^Th)\prod_i\exp(v_id_i)$, and summing over binary $v$ gives $\exp(b^Th)\prod_i(1+\exp(d_i))$. Hence $p(v\mid h)$ is the product of Bernoulli masses with success probabilities $\exp(d_i)/(1+\exp(d_i))=\sigma(d_i)$. [given, step 1.1, algebra]

2.3 For fixed observed $v$, $p(v)=Z^{-1}\exp(a^Tv)\sum_h\exp(b^Th+v^TWh)$. Differentiating these finite sums gives $\partial_{W_{ij}}\log p(v)=v_i\mathbb E_{p(h\mid v)}[h_j]-\partial_{W_{ij}}\log Z$; the same calculation gives $\partial_{a_i}\log p(v)=v_i-\partial_{a_i}\log Z$ and $\partial_{b_j}\log p(v)=\mathbb E_{p(h\mid v)}[h_j]-\partial_{b_j}\log Z$. [F3, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 The product conditional mass functions in steps 2.1–1.3 make the conditional expectations of any bounded measurable functions of disjoint coordinates factor into the product of their conditional expectations. By [F1]–[F2], each layer is therefore conditionally independent given the other in the stated sigma-algebra sense. This use of the conditional-expectation convention is the only proof point needing [A1]. [F1, F2, A1, step 2.1, step 2.2]

3.2 Differentiating the finite partition sum yields $\partial_{W_{ij}}\log Z=\sum_{v',h'}v_i'h_j'p(v',h')=\mathbb E_p[V_iH_j]$, $\partial_{a_i}\log Z=\mathbb E_p[V_i]$, and $\partial_{b_j}\log Z=\mathbb E_p[H_j]$. Substitution in step 2.3 gives the exact gradients in the Definition. [F3, step 2.3, algebra]

4.1 For each visible state $v$, $\sum_{v'}K(v,v')=\sum_h p(h\mid v)\sum_{v'}p(v'\mid h)=\sum_hp(h\mid v)=1$. Thus K is a stochastic matrix and each $q_k^v$ is a well-defined finite probability distribution. Replacing the exact negative-phase marginal $p(v')$ in the gradient formulas by $q_k^v(v')$ gives the finite contrastive-divergence statistic defined in the Statement. [step 2.1, step 2.2, step 3.2, algebra] ∎

**Given:** Metric spaces, a compact subset $K$, continuous maps, and uniform convergence on $K$ as stated.

[F1] Compactness means that every open cover has a finite subcover; this convention applies to compact subsets of metric spaces ([[def-metric-compactness]]).

[F2] A continuous map sends a compact subset of a metric space to a compact subset ([[thm-continuous-image-of-a-compact-space-is-compact]]).

[F3] In a metric space, open sets contain an open ball about each of their points, and open balls are open ([[def-metric-space]], [[def-metric-topology]]).



**Proof technique:** open-cover argument with a uniform neighborhood of the limit image.

1.1 If $K=\emptyset$, then $W=\emptyset$ and it is compact. Otherwise let $\mathcal V$ be any open cover of $W$. By [F2], $f[K]$ is compact, so [F1] gives finitely many $V_1,\ldots,V_q\in\mathcal V$ covering $f[K]$. Set $O=\bigcup_{i=1}^qV_i$, an open set containing $f[K]$. [given, F1, F2, cases]

2.1 Form the family of all balls $B_Y(y,r)$ with $y\in f[K]$, $r>0$, and $B_Y(y,2r)\subseteq O$. This family covers $f[K]$ by openness and [F3], so [F1] gives a finite subcover with centers $y_1,\ldots,y_s$ and radii $r_1,\ldots,r_s$. Since $f[K]\ne\emptyset$, $s\ge1$; let $\delta=\min_i r_i>0$. If $z\in Y$ and $d_Y(z,y)<\delta$ for some $y\in f[K]$, choose $i$ with $d_Y(y,y_i)<r_i$; then $d_Y(z,y_i)<\delta+r_i\le2r_i$, so $z\in B_Y(y_i,2r_i)\subseteq O$. Thus every point within distance $\delta$ of some point of $f[K]$ lies in $O$. [step 1.1, F1, F3, algebra]

3.1 Uniform convergence supplies $N\ge1$ such that $d_Y(f_n(x),f(x))<\delta$ for every $x\in K$ and every $n\ge N$. Since $f(x)\in f[K]$, step 2.1 implies $f_n[K]\subseteq O$ for every $n\ge N$. [given, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 For each of the finitely many indices $1\le n<N$, [F2] makes $f_n[K]$ compact, so [F1] supplies a finite subfamily of $\mathcal V$ covering it. Together with $V_1,\ldots,V_q$ from step 1.1, these finitely many members cover $f[K]$, all $f_n[K]$ with $n\ge N$, and each remaining $f_n[K]$. Hence every open cover of $W$ has a finite subcover, so $W$ is compact by [F1]. The proof uses only finite subcovers and a finite minimum, not a choice axiom. [step 1.1, step 3.1, F1, F2, algebra] ∎

**Given:** Probability vectors $r,s,q,q'$ on a finite alphabet, with $\|q-q'\|_1\le\epsilon$.



1.1 Put $\bar r=(r+s)/2$ and $\bar q=(q+q')/2$. For every $a\in\Sigma$, $q(a)\le\bar q(a)+\epsilon$ and $q'(a)\le\bar q(a)+\epsilon$. Define $w(a)=(\bar q(a)+\epsilon)/(1+m\epsilon)$; its coordinates are nonnegative and sum to one. Monotonicity of $-\log$ on positive reals gives $\frac12\operatorname{CE}(r,q)+\frac12\operatorname{CE}(s,q')\ge \operatorname{CE}(\bar r,w)-\log(1+m\epsilon)$. If a term on the left is infinite, the claimed inequality is immediate; otherwise this comparison is valid on each target-positive coordinate. [given, construct, algebra]

2.1 For any probability vectors $\bar r,w$, if $w(a)=0<\bar r(a)$ then $\operatorname{CE}(\bar r,w)=+\infty$. Otherwise $\operatorname{CE}(\bar r,w)-H(\bar r)=\sum_{a:\bar r(a)>0}\bar r(a)\log(\bar r(a)/w(a))\ge0$: applying $\log t\le t-1$ to $t=w(a)/\bar r(a)$ gives the sum at least $\sum_{a:\bar r(a)>0}(\bar r(a)-w(a))\ge0$. Combining with step 1.1 proves the bound. [step 1.1, given, algebra] ∎

**Given:** A probability measure $\mu$ on nonempty $X$, an integer $d\ge1$, and a constant $c>0$.

[F1] A probability measure satisfies $\mu(X)=1$ ([[def-probability-measure]]).

[F2] If $E\subseteq X$ is measurable, then $\mu(E)\le\mu(X)$ ([[prop-measure-monotonicity]]).



**Proof technique:** choose one scale at which the asserted lower bound exceeds total mass.

1.1 Choose $\varepsilon>c^{-1/d}$. Since $X$ is nonempty, any partition of $X$ has at least one cell $E$. The set $E$ is measurable and $E\subseteq X$, so [F1] and [F2] give $\mu(E)\le1$. [given, F1, F2, choose]

2.1 The asserted lower bound gives $\mu(E)\ge c\varepsilon^d>1$, contradicting step 1.1. Hence no such all-scale family of partitions exists. [given, step 1.1, algebra, contradiction] ∎

**Given:** The inputs and instructions in the Definition.

[F1] The objective convention uses a symmetric positive-semidefinite sample covariance input and $\lambda>0$. [[def-graphical-lasso-objective]].

[F2] Every real symmetric matrix has an orthonormal eigenbasis. [[cor-real-spectral-theorem-for-self-adjoint-endomorphisms]].



**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 For any nonzero $x\in\mathbb R^p$, $x^TWx=x^TSx+\lambda\|x\|^2\ge\lambda\|x\|^2>0$, so the initialized $W$ is symmetric positive definite. [given, F1, algebra]

2.1 Suppose the current $W$ is positive definite. Its principal submatrix $V$ is positive definite, so $V_{\ell\ell}>0$ for each coordinate. With other coordinates fixed, the lasso objective $\tfrac12\beta^TV\beta-s^T\beta+\lambda\|\beta\|_1$ as a function of $\beta_\ell=t$ is $\tfrac12V_{\ell\ell}t^2-rt+\lambda|t|+\text{constant}$, where $r=s_\ell-\sum_{k\ne\ell}V_{\ell k}\beta_k$. Its unique minimizer is $(r-\lambda)/V_{\ell\ell}$ when $r>\lambda$, zero when $|r|\le\lambda$, and $(r+\lambda)/V_{\ell\ell}$ when $r<-\lambda$, exactly the displayed soft-threshold update. Hence every finite coordinate sweep is well-defined. [F1, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 Each block candidate is a finite symmetric matrix. By [F2] it has a symmetric eigendecomposition, and all its eigenvalues are positive exactly when it is positive definite. The procedure accepts only candidates passing this finite test, so positive definiteness is invariant until either an explicit failure is returned or all $Rp$ blocks finish. [F2, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 The fixed positive integers $R$ and $K$ bound all outer and inner loops, so the procedure terminates. On success the final $W$ is positive definite by step 3.1, hence $W^{-1}$ exists and is positive definite. The procedure makes no conclusion that this truncated output maximizes $F_{S,\lambda}$ or that increasing $R$ and $K$ converges. [given, step 3.1, algebra] ∎

**Given:** AC, the independent column vectors $Y_{n,j}$, and the fixed parameter $z$ with $\operatorname{Im}z=\eta>0$.

[A1] The Axiom of Choice states every family of nonempty sets has a choice function ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]).

[F1] For a real symmetric non-negative matrix, adding one rank-one matrix $yy^{\mathsf T}$ changes the unnormalized resolvent trace by at most $1/\eta$ ([[lem-rank-one-resolvent-update-and-trace-bound]]).

[F2] For independent random elements and a real measurable function whose change under replacement of coordinate $j$ is at most $c_j$, the two-sided McDiarmid bound is $2\exp(-2t^2/\sum_jc_j^2)$ ([[thm-mcdiarmid-bounded-differences]]).

[F3] If $\sum_n\Pr(E_n)<\infty$, then almost surely only finitely many $E_n$ occur ([[cor-first-borel-cantelli-lemma-for-events]]).



**Given:** The hypotheses and notation of the Statement, including AC.

1.1 Fix all vectors except $Y_{n,j}$. Replacing that vector by another vector $Y'_{n,j}$ changes $B_n$ by removing $Y_{n,j}Y_{n,j}^{\mathsf T}$ and adding $Y'_{n,j}Y_{n,j}^{\mathsf T}$. Applying [F1] once to remove the first term and once to add the second shows that $\operatorname{tr}(B_n-zI)^{-1}$ changes by at most $2/\eta$. Hence each of the real and imaginary parts of $M_n(z)$ has coordinate oscillation at most $c_j=2/(d_n\eta)$. [given, F1, algebra]

1.2 Apply [F2] separately to $\operatorname{Re}M_n(z)$ and $\operatorname{Im}M_n(z)$. If a complex number has modulus greater than $t$, at least one of its real or imaginary parts has magnitude greater than $t/\sqrt2$. The union bound therefore gives
$$\Pr\{|M_n(z)-\mathbb E M_n(z)|>t\}
\le4\exp\left(-\frac{t^2d_n^2\eta^2}{4N_n}\right).$$
This is the stated estimate. [A1, F2, step 1.1, algebra]

2.1 Since $d_n/n\to c>0$, for each fixed $t>0$ the exponent in step 1.2 is at most $-c_tn$ for all sufficiently large $n$, for some $c_t>0$. The probabilities are therefore summable. [given, step 1.2, algebra]

3.1 Apply [F3] to the events in step 2.1 for each $t=1/k$, $k\ge1$, and intersect the resulting countable collection of probability-one events. On that event $M_n(z)-\mathbb E M_n(z)\to0$. [F3, step 2.1, choose] ∎

**Given:** AC, $p\ge2$, a random vector $X$ with law $N_p(\mu,\Sigma)$, and real symmetric positive-definite $\Sigma$.

[F1] A multivariate normal law has the scalar normal projections prescribed by its mean and covariance, including the covariance of every linear projection. [[def-multivariate-normal-law]].

[F2] When $\Sigma$ is positive definite, the law has density $(2\pi)^{-p/2}\det(\Sigma)^{-1/2}\exp(-\tfrac12(x-\mu)^T\Sigma^{-1}(x-\mu))$. [[thm-nondegenerate-multivariate-normal-law-has-density]].

[F3] For a joint density with positive finite marginal sections, normalizing each section gives a regular conditional distribution of the first coordinate given the second. [[thm-conditional-density-formula]].

[F4] Conditional independence given a sigma-algebra is factorization of conditional expectations for every pair of bounded measurable real functions. [[def-conditional-independence-given-a-sigma-algebra]].

[F5] A scalar $N(m,s^2)$ law has characteristic function $\exp(itm-\tfrac12s^2t^2)$. [[lem-characteristic-function-of-a-normal-law]].

[F6] On Borel subsets of $\mathbb R^{r+s}$, product Lebesgue measure agrees with Euclidean Lebesgue measure under countable choice. [[thm-lebesgue-product-measure-agrees-with-euclidean-lebesgue-on-borel-sets]] [[def-countable-choice]].

[F7] AC implies countable choice. [[lem-ac-supplies-sequential-choices-for-probability-constructions]].

[F8] The pairwise Markov property tests conditional independence exactly at nonedges of a finite simple undirected graph. [[def-undirected-graphical-model-and-markov-properties]].

[A1] AC is the explicit hypothesis of the conditional-independence convention, and here means that every family of nonempty sets has a choice function. [[def-conditional-independence-given-a-sigma-algebra]] [[def-axiom-of-choice]].



1.1 Fix distinct $i,j$. By [A1], [F1] and [F2], the joint density of $X$ is the stated nondegenerate Gaussian density; here positive definiteness is an additional hypothesis beyond the singular-covariance multivariate-normal definition. [given, A1, F1, F2]

2.1 Reorder coordinates so $Y=(X_i,X_j)$ and $Z=(X_k)_{k\notin\{i,j\}}$. In the correspondingly permuted precision matrix write $\Theta=\begin{pmatrix}A&B\\B^T&C\end{pmatrix}$, where $A=\begin{pmatrix}a&c\\c&d\end{pmatrix}$. For every nonzero $u\in\mathbb R^2$, $u^TAu=(u,0)^T\Theta(u,0)>0$, so $A$ is positive definite and $\det A=ad-c^2>0$. If $p=2$, the $Z$ coordinate is a singleton and the following conditional-density calculation is the unconditional bivariate density. [step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 For $p>2$, [F7] supplies the countable-choice hypothesis of [F6], so the joint Euclidean density in [F2] is also a density relative to $\lambda_2\otimes\lambda_{p-2}$. Put $u=y-\mu_Y$, $w=z-\mu_Z$, and $D=C-B^TA^{-1}B$. For nonzero $w$, $(-A^{-1}Bw,w)^T\Theta(-A^{-1}Bw,w)=w^TDw>0$, hence $D$ is positive definite. Completing the square gives $u^TAu+2u^TBw+w^TCw=(u+A^{-1}Bw)^TA(u+A^{-1}Bw)+w^TDw$. The section integral over $y$ is therefore positive and finite for every $z$: its $y$ factor is the normalized two-dimensional Gaussian density with precision $A$, multiplied by a finite positive constant. [step 2.1, F2, F6, F7, algebra]

4.1 For $p>2$, use the explicit filler probability concentrated at $(0,0)$ on $\mathbb R^2$ in [F3]; the positive finite marginal sections from step 3.1 show that the conditional law at every $z$ has density $\frac{\sqrt{\det A}}{2\pi}\exp(-\tfrac12(u+A^{-1}Bw)^TA(u+A^{-1}Bw))$. It is the bivariate normal law with mean $\mu_Y-A^{-1}B(z-\mu_Z)$ and covariance $A^{-1}$. For $p=2$, this is the unconditional law with covariance $\Theta^{-1}=A^{-1}$. [step 2.1, step 3.1, F2, F3]

5.1 If $\Theta_{ij}=c=0$, then $A$ is diagonal and the conditional density in step 4.1 is a product of two univariate Gaussian densities for every $z$. Its conditional expectations therefore factor for all bounded measurable coordinate functions; [F4] gives $X_i\perp\!\!\!\perp X_j\mid\sigma(Z)$. [step 4.1, F4, algebra]

5.2 Conversely, suppose $X_i\perp\!\!\!\perp X_j\mid\sigma(Z)$. Apply [F4] to the four bounded pairs formed from $\cos(X_i),\sin(X_i)$ and $\cos(X_j),\sin(X_j)$ and combine the resulting identities. For almost every $z$, the conditional joint characteristic function at $(1,1)$ equals the product of its conditional marginal characteristic functions. By [F1], [F4] and [F5], the joint characteristic function from step 4.1 is $\exp(i(m_1(z)+m_2(z))-\tfrac12((A^{-1})_{11}+2(A^{-1})_{12}+(A^{-1})_{22}))$, whereas that product omits the middle covariance term. Equality implies $\exp(-(A^{-1})_{12})=1$, and since $(A^{-1})_{12}$ is real this forces $(A^{-1})_{12}=0$. [step 4.1, F1, F4, F5]

6.1 The inverse of $A$ is $(ad-c^2)^{-1}\begin{pmatrix}d&-c\\-c&a\end{pmatrix}$. Since $\det A>0$, $(A^{-1})_{12}=0$ if and only if $c=0$, which is exactly $\Theta_{ij}=0$. Steps 5.1 and 5.2 prove the two implications; by [F8], these are exactly the nonedge and conditional-independence cases of the Gaussian pairwise Markov graph. [step 2.1, step 5.1, step 5.2, F8, algebra] ∎

**Given:** $p\ge1$, $S\in\mathbb S_+^p$, $\lambda>0$, and the symmetric positive-definite domain and all-entry objective in the Statement.

[F1] The all-entry graphical-lasso functional is $F_{S,\lambda}(\Theta)=\log\det\Theta-\operatorname{tr}(S\Theta)-\lambda\sum_{i,j}|\Theta_{ij}|$ on $\mathbb S_{++}^p$. [[def-graphical-lasso-objective]].

[F2] A finite-dimensional nonnegative self-adjoint operator has a factorization $S=R^*R$. [[thm-non-negative-operator-characterisations]].

[F3] A real symmetric matrix has an orthonormal eigenbasis. [[cor-real-spectral-theorem-for-self-adjoint-endomorphisms]].

[F4] For a twice continuously differentiable function on an open convex Euclidean domain, positive-semidefinite Hessian everywhere implies convexity. [[thm-hessian-characterises-convexity]].

[F5] Convexity on a convex set is the chord inequality; strict convexity requires strict inequality for distinct points and interior weights. [[def-convex-and-strictly-convex-functions-on-euclidean-sets]].



1.1 By the all-entry objective definition [F1] and the nonnegative-operator factorization [F2], write $S=R^TR$. Thus $\operatorname{tr}(S\Theta)=\operatorname{tr}(R\Theta R^T)\ge0$ for $\Theta\succ0$. Also $\|\Theta\|_1=\sum_{i,j}|\Theta_{ij}|\ge\sum_i\Theta_{ii}=\operatorname{tr}\Theta$, since positive-definite matrices have positive diagonal entries. [given, F1, F2, algebra]

1.2 The cone $\mathbb S_{++}^p$ is open and convex: positive quadratic forms remain positive under sufficiently small symmetric perturbations, and convex combinations of positive quadratic forms remain positive. For symmetric $H$, determinant expansion gives $\left.\frac{d}{dt}\log\det(\Theta+tH)\right|_{t=0}=\operatorname{tr}(\Theta^{-1}H)$. Differentiating $(\Theta+tH)(\Theta+tH)^{-1}=I$ gives $\left.\frac{d}{dt}(\Theta+tH)^{-1}\right|_{t=0}=-\Theta^{-1}H\Theta^{-1}$, so the second directional derivative is $-\operatorname{tr}(\Theta^{-1}H\Theta^{-1}H)$. [given, F3, algebra]

2.1 By [F3], the eigenvalues $t_1,\ldots,t_p$ of $\Theta\succ0$ are positive and $\log\det\Theta=\sum_k\log t_k$, $\operatorname{tr}\Theta=\sum_k t_k$. Hence $F_{S,\lambda}(\Theta)\le\sum_{k=1}^p h(t_k)$ for $h(t)=\log t-\lambda t$. The function $h$ is bounded above and tends to $-\infty$ as $t\downarrow0$ or $t\to\infty$. For any $c$, the upper level set $F_{S,\lambda}(\Theta)\ge c$ therefore forces each eigenvalue into a compact interval $[a_c,b_c]\subset(0,\infty)$: if $M=\sup_{t>0}h(t)$, then each $h(t_k)\ge c-(p-1)M$. These matrices form a closed bounded set of symmetric matrices contained in $\mathbb S_{++}^p$, hence a compact set. Taking $c=F_{S,\lambda}(I)$ gives a nonempty compact upper level set, and continuity of $F$ yields a maximizer. [step 1.1, F3, algebra]

2.2 Let $B=\Theta^{-1/2}H\Theta^{-1/2}$, using the positive square root from the orthonormal eigenbasis [F3]. Then $B$ is symmetric and $\operatorname{tr}(\Theta^{-1}H\Theta^{-1}H)=\operatorname{tr}(B^2)=\|B\|_F^2$, strictly positive when $H\ne0$. Thus the second derivative of $\log\det$ along every nonconstant segment is strictly negative, giving its strict chord inequality. The Hessian of $-\log\det$ is positive semidefinite by step 1.2, so [F4] gives convexity in the chord sense of [F5]. The trace term is linear and the entrywise $\ell^1$ norm is convex by the triangle inequality, so its negative is concave; adding these terms preserves the strict chord inequality. Hence $F_{S,\lambda}$ is strictly concave on its open convex domain. [F3, F4, F5, step 1.2, algebra]

2.3 Put $G=\Theta^{-1}-S$. At a maximizer every feasible one-coordinate directional derivative is at most zero, and when the objective is differentiable in both directions its derivative is zero. Since $\Theta_{ii}>0$, the diagonal penalty is locally differentiable with slope $1$, so the diagonal equation is $G_{ii}-\lambda=0$ and $\Gamma_{ii}=1$. For $i<j$, a symmetric perturbation by $t(E_{ij}+E_{ji})$ has smooth derivative $2G_{ij}t$ and changes the penalty by $2\lambda(|\Theta_{ij}+t|-|\Theta_{ij}|)$. If $\Theta_{ij}\ne0$, testing both signs of small $t$ gives $G_{ij}=\lambda\operatorname{sign}(\Theta_{ij})$. If $\Theta_{ij}=0$, taking $t>0$ gives $G_{ij}\le\lambda$ and taking $t<0$ gives $G_{ij}\ge-\lambda$. Defining $\Gamma_{ij}=\Gamma_{ji}=G_{ij}/\lambda$ at zero and the sign otherwise yields the stated KKT equation for the all-entry penalty [F1]. [given, F1, step 1.2, algebra]

3.1 Conversely, suppose $\Theta\succ0$ and a symmetric $\Gamma$ satisfies the stated entrywise conditions and $\Theta^{-1}-S-\lambda\Gamma=0$. Put $T=\Theta^{-1/2}\Theta'\Theta^{-1/2}$ for any $\Theta'\succ0$; its eigenvalues $t_r$ are positive. Since $\log t\le t-1$ for $t>0$ (the function $t-1-\log t$ has its minimum $0$ at $t=1$), $\log\det\Theta'-\log\det\Theta=\sum_r\log t_r\le\operatorname{tr}(T)-p=\operatorname{tr}(\Theta^{-1}(\Theta'-\Theta))$. For each scalar $x$ and each allowed subgradient $\gamma$ of $|x|$, $|y|\ge|x|+\gamma(y-x)$: if $x\ne0$, this follows from $|y|\ge\operatorname{sign}(x)y$, while for $x=0$ it follows from $|\gamma|\le1$. Summing gives $\|\Theta'\|_1\ge\|\Theta\|_1+\sum_{i,j}\Gamma_{ij}(\Theta'_{ij}-\Theta_{ij})$ for the all-entry objective [F1]. Combining these bounds with the linear trace term and the KKT equation yields $F_{S,\lambda}(\Theta')-F_{S,\lambda}(\Theta)\le\operatorname{tr}((\Theta^{-1}-S-\lambda\Gamma)(\Theta'-\Theta))=0$. Thus every such KKT point is a maximizer. The maximizer exists by step 2.1 and is unique by strict concavity from step 2.2, so the KKT condition is both necessary and sufficient for that unique optimum. [given, F1, step 2.1, step 2.2, step 2.3, algebra] ∎

**Given:** $0<\alpha<1$ and the source's claimed $C^{2,\alpha}(U)\cap C^0(\bar U)$ solution class.

[F1] The library's $C^{2,\alpha}(U)$ is the bounded global Hölder class; its norm includes the supremum of every second derivative over all of $U$ ([[def-holder-spaces-c-k-alpha-and-their-scaled-norms]]).

[F2] For $L=\Delta$, a bounded-domain function $w\in C^2(U)\cap C^0(\bar U)$ with $\Delta w=0$ and $w|_{\partial U}=0$ vanishes identically ([[lem-shin-elliptic-residual-stability]]).

[F3] The locally proved radial profile $\chi$ is smooth, equals $1$ for $r\le1/4$, and equals $0$ for $r\ge1/2$ ([[lem-shin-radial-smooth-cutoff]]).

[F4] The Laplacian of a scalar $C^2$ function on an open subset of $\mathbb R^2$ is $w_{xx}+w_{yy}$ ([[def-laplacian-of-a-c2-function]]).

[F5] The total chain rule applies to the smooth local polar-coordinate change on $r>0$ ([[thm-chain-rule-for-total-derivatives]]).



1.1 Let $U=\{(r\cos\theta,r\sin\theta):0<r<1,\ 0<\theta<2\pi/3\}$. It is bounded and Lipschitz: its boundary consists of two line segments and a circular arc, meeting at finitely many corners of angles $2\pi/3$ and $\pi/2$. At a smooth boundary point, a sufficiently small ball tangent on the exterior side is disjoint from $U$; on the circular arc one can use a ball outside the unit disk. At a corner of interior angle $\beta<\pi$, choose a ball tangent at the corner with its center on the exterior angle bisector. Directions from the vertex to points in this ball lie within angle $\pi/2$ of the center direction, while the sector directions are at angular distance at least $\pi-\beta/2>\pi/2$; hence the ball is exterior. Therefore $U$ satisfies the exterior sphere condition everywhere. [given, cases]

1.2 Let $\chi$ be the profile supplied by [F3]. Set
$$u(r,\theta)=\chi(r)r^{3/2}\sin(3\theta/2),\qquad L=\Delta,\qquad f=\Delta u,\qquad g=0.$$
